skill.name: Precise word for a vague one
skill.why: Vague words like nice make readers guess. A precise word shows what you mean.
skill.how: Spot the vague word. Hunt for clues. Pick the word that fits every clue.

beats.say: Nice is a vague word. Nice how?

beats.show: It **warmed me up** on a **freezing day**.

beats.say: Chilled? No, it warmed me up. Spicy? No clue says so.
Steaming fits every clue. That's the precise word!

weDo.text: Gus put the thing on the table. It had pages and a hard cover.
weDo.hint: What has pages and a hard cover?
weDo.success: Book. Pages and a hard cover tell you exactly what the thing is.

options.reason: A plate doesn't have pages.
A box can have a hard lid, but it doesn't have pages.

weDo.hint: Which word could mean almost anything?
weDo.success: Stuff. It could mean anything at all, so the reader has no idea what else the kelpie herded.

parts.reason: Kelpie is precise. It names the exact kind of dog.
Eleven is precise. It tells you the exact number.

creature.name: Spikkit
creature.blurb: A sacred kingfisher that only dives when it can see exactly the right fish. Give it a blurry word and it stays on its branch.

encounters.frame: Mo is writing a review of his own cooking. Again.
encounters.text: Mo's pie was bad. The middle was still frozen solid.
encounters.prompt: Which word says exactly what was wrong with the pie?
encounters.success: Undercooked. A frozen middle means it wasn't cooked for long enough.

options.reason: Burnt means cooked for too long. Would a burnt pie still be frozen in the middle?
Soggy means wet and floppy. Frozen solid means hard.

encounters.frame: Zed is posting his scores on the class board.
encounters.prompt: Tap the vague word that doesn't tell you exactly how Zed did.
encounters.success: Good. It doesn't tell you the score, so the reader can't tell if Zed did OK or broke a record.

parts.reason: Score is precise. It names exactly what Zed got.
Final is precise. It tells you exactly which round.

encounters.frame: Wren is writing up her zoo trip.
encounters.text: Wren saw a big animal at the zoo. It had a long trunk and huge flappy ears.
encounters.prompt: Which word could replace 'big animal'?
encounters.success: Elephant. A long trunk and huge flappy ears tell you exactly which animal it was.

options.reason: A giraffe has a long neck, not a trunk.
A rhino has a horn and small ears, not a trunk.

encounters.frame: A Spikkit only dives for the most precise word. Line them up for it.
encounters.prompt: Put the words in order, from the vaguest to the most precise.
encounters.success: A rainbow lorikeet is a parrot, a parrot is a bird, and a bird is an animal.

body.reason: Start with the word that covers the most things. Each next word is a kind of the one before.

encounters.frame: Indi stuck a sign up next to her new artwork.
encounters.prompt: Tap the vague word, then choose a precise one.
encounters.success: Mural. A mural is a picture painted on a wall, so wet paint makes sense.

parts.reason: Touch is fine. It says exactly what not to do.

parts: on the wall. The paint is still

parts.reason: Wet is precise. It tells you why you shouldn't touch.

options.reason: A photo isn't painted, so it can't have wet paint.
A mirror is glass, not wet paint.

encounters.frame: The Spikkit is sorting fish. Blurry ones go back in the water.
encounters.prompt: Match each word to the right bucket.
encounters.success: Vague words could mean lots of things. Precise words mean one exact thing.

items.reason: Stuff could mean almost anything, so it's vague.
Nice tells you something is good, but not how. It's vague.
Thing could be any object at all, so it's vague.
Sprint means run as fast as you can, so it's precise.
Spatula names one exact kitchen tool, so it's precise.
Drizzling means light, fine rain. That's precise.
Kelpie names one exact kind of dog, so it's precise.

encounters.frame: Indi is writing about her first swim of the year.
encounters.text: The water was cold. Indi's toes went numb as soon as she stepped in.
encounters.prompt: Which word says exactly how cold the water was?
encounters.success: Icy. Toes going numb straight away tells you the water was extremely cold.

options.reason: Cool means only a little cold. Cool water wouldn't make your toes go numb straight away.
Lukewarm means a bit warm. It wouldn't make anyone's toes go numb.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing instructions for his new robot.
encounters.prompt: Tap the vague word that Gus should replace.
encounters.success: Thing. The reader can't picture it, so Gus should name exactly what's on the robot's head.

parts.reason: Robot is precise enough. You know exactly what Gus built.
Spins is precise. It tells you exactly how it moves.
Beeps is precise. It tells you exactly what sound it makes.

encounters.frame: Tully's match report has a vague word about the weather.
encounters.prompt: Tap the vague word, then choose a precise one.
encounters.success: Gusty. A hat blowing into the crowd tells you the wind was strong and came in bursts.

parts.reason: Umpire's is precise. It tells you exactly whose hat it was.
Crowd is fine. It tells you where the hat ended up.

options.reason: Drizzly means light rain. Rain doesn't blow a hat into the crowd.
Foggy means it was hard to see. Fog doesn't blow a hat away.

encounters.frame: Zed is complaining about his new speaker.
encounters.text: Zed's speaker made a weird noise. It was high and sharp, like a pig squealing.
encounters.prompt: Which word says exactly what the noise was?
encounters.success: Screech. A screech is a high, sharp sound, just like a pig squealing.

options.reason: A rumble is a deep, low sound. This noise was high and sharp.
A hum is a soft, steady sound. A squealing pig isn't soft.

encounters.frame: Tully is training a Spikkit to go from blurry to sharp.
encounters.prompt: Put the words in order, from the vaguest to the most precise.
encounters.success: A fire truck is a kind of truck, a truck is a vehicle, and a vehicle is a thing.

body.reason: Start with the word that could mean the most things. Each next word is a kind of the one before.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing up what he found under his bed.
encounters.prompt: Match each precise word to the vague word it could replace.
encounters.success: Soaked, drenched and damp all say how wet. Putrid, musty and rank all say how smelly.

items.reason: Soaked means wet right through.
Damp means a little bit wet.
Drenched means completely wet, as if you've been in a downpour.
Putrid means smelling of something rotting.
Musty means smelling old and stale, like a cupboard nobody has opened for years.
Rank means smelling strong and nasty.

encounters.frame: Gus left his footy socks in the rain overnight.
encounters.text: Gus's sock was wet. When he squeezed it, water poured out and splashed all over the floor.
encounters.prompt: Which word says exactly how wet the sock was?
encounters.success: Soaked. Water pouring out when you squeeze it means the sock was wet right through.

options.reason: Damp means only a little wet. Water wouldn't pour out of a damp sock.
Moist means slightly wet. Water wouldn't splash all over the floor.
Humid describes air that feels heavy with water, not a sock.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing up his night in the old house.
encounters.text: The noise in the attic was quiet. Zed had to hold his breath to hear it at all.
encounters.prompt: Which word says exactly what the noise was like?
encounters.success: Faint. A faint sound is so quiet you can only just hear it, which is why Zed held his breath.

options.reason: Silent means no sound at all. Zed could hear it, just barely.
Shrill means high and piercing. You wouldn't need to hold your breath to hear it.
Booming means loud and deep. Zed could hardly hear this noise.

encounters.frame: The school newsletter is writing about Indi's work.
encounters.prompt: Tap the vague word that wastes the reader's time.
encounters.success: Thing. The rest of the sentence shows it's a mural, so 'thing' tells the reader nothing.

parts.reason: Giant is precise. It tells you the painting is very big.
Whale is precise. It names exactly what the painting shows.
Whole is precise. It tells you exactly how much of the wall it covers.

encounters.frame: Mo's curry review uses a word that could mean two things.
encounters.prompt: Tap the vague word, then choose a precise one.
encounters.success: Spicy. The curry came cold from the fridge, so it was hot with chilli spice, not heat.

parts.reason: Curry is precise. It names exactly what Mo served.

parts: cold, straight from the fridge. It was so

parts.reason: Chilli is precise, and it's the clue. Look for the word that could mean two things.
Water is fine. Watery eyes are what chilli does to you.

options.reason: Steaming means hot enough to give off steam. This curry came cold from the fridge.
Scalding means hot enough to burn your skin. This curry came cold from the fridge.
Sizzling means hot and hissing in the pan. This curry came cold from the fridge.

encounters.frame: Zed is sharpening the words in his space project.
encounters.prompt: Match each precise word to the vague word it could replace.
encounters.success: Colossal, immense and vast sharpen big. Microscopic and minuscule sharpen small. Dazzling and blinding sharpen bright.

items.reason: Colossal means enormous, so it sharpens big.
Immense means hugely big, so it sharpens big.
Vast means huge and spread out, like space itself, so it sharpens big.
Microscopic means so small you need a microscope, so it sharpens small.
Minuscule means extremely small, so it sharpens small.
Dazzling means so bright it's hard to look at, so it sharpens bright.
Blinding means bright enough to stop you seeing, so it sharpens bright.

encounters.frame: Tully is describing his lucky footy jumper.
encounters.text: Tully's jumper was old. It had holes in both elbows, and the threads on the cuffs had come loose.
encounters.prompt: Which word matches the clues exactly?
encounters.success: Tattered. Tattered means old and torn, with holes and loose threads.

options.reason: Faded means the colour has gone pale. The clues are about holes and loose threads, not colour.
Antique means very old and valuable, usually over a hundred years. Nothing says the jumper is that old.
Shrunken means it has got smaller in the wash. The clues are about holes, not size.

encounters.frame: The lighthouse keeper's logbook needs one sharper word.
encounters.text: The sea was rough that morning. Waves the size of houses smashed against the cliffs and flung spray over the lighthouse.
encounters.prompt: Which word matches the clues exactly?
encounters.success: Mountainous. Waves the size of houses are towering, which is exactly what mountainous means.

options.reason: Placid means calm and still. This sea was smashing against cliffs.
Glassy means smooth and flat, like glass. This sea was smashing against cliffs.
Rippling means covered in tiny waves. These waves were huge.

encounters.frame: Gus has edited his robot's repair log, but he missed one vague word.
encounters.prompt: Tap the word that is still vague after Gus's edit.
encounters.success: Stuff. Every other word tells you exactly what happened, but 'stuff' hides what the robot did to the engine.

parts.reason: Titanium is precise. It names exactly what the robot is made of.
Cracked is precise. It tells you exactly what was wrong with the hull.
Nine is precise. It tells you exactly how many minutes.

encounters.prompt: Tap the vague words, then choose a precise one.

parts.reason: Vet is precise. It tells you exactly who checked the wombat.
Back leg is precise. It tells you exactly where the injury was.

parts: . It was long and deep and needed

parts.reason: Twelve is precise. It tells you exactly how many stitches.

A sprain is a twisted joint. You can't stitch a sprain.

encounters.frame: Maxx Vantablack is bragging on his channel. Wren checks the numbers.
encounters.text: Maxx claimed that 'heaps' of people watched his live stream. The counter showed exactly twelve viewers, and one of them was his mum.
encounters.prompt: Which words tell the truth about how many people watched?
encounters.success: A dozen. A dozen means exactly twelve, which is what the counter showed.

options.reason: Dozens of means at least twenty-four. The counter showed only twelve.
Hundreds of is even more of an exaggeration than 'heaps'. The counter showed twelve.
A pair means two. The counter showed twelve viewers.

encounters.frame: Indi is labelling the sounds from Zed's band practice.
encounters.prompt: Match each precise word to the vague word it could replace.
encounters.success: Thunderous and blaring sharpen loud. Hushed and muted sharpen quiet. Sluggish and unhurried sharpen slow.

items.reason: Thunderous means as loud as thunder, so it sharpens loud.
Blaring means harshly loud, like a car horn, so it sharpens loud.
Hushed means made quiet on purpose, like a crowd before a solo.
Muted means softened and quiet, so it sharpens quiet.
Sluggish means slow and lacking energy, so it sharpens slow.
Unhurried means slow and relaxed, never rushing, so it sharpens slow.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing a review of the hardest game he has ever played.
encounters.text: Zed's new game is hard. Even the first level takes most players over a hundred tries, and nobody in the world has finished it yet.
encounters.prompt: Which word matches the clues exactly?
encounters.success: Brutal. A brutal game is punishingly difficult, which fits a hundred tries and nobody finishing.

options.reason: A forgiving game goes easy on your mistakes. A hundred tries on level one is the opposite.
Confusing means hard to understand. The clues say it's hard to beat, not hard to understand.
Glitchy means full of bugs. Nothing in the clues says the game is broken.
